title: Grace Aguilar
hookLine: a nineteenth-century English Jewish writer and teacher

cards: A young woman in England sits at a desk, a Bible open and a pen in her hand. She is Jewish, from a family whose ancestors, the family remembered, had once hidden their Judaism in Portugal to survive.

Around her, English Jewish girls are growing up reading English books, and some of the books about the Bible they can read in their own language were written by people hoping to persuade them to leave Judaism.
She has a simple thought: our women should hear the Bible's women from one of their own. Her name is Grace Aguilar, and she picks up the pen.

teach.h: SHE WROTE IN ENGLISH, FOR JEWS.
teach.b: Grace Aguilar lived in the nineteenth century and wrote in English, for English-speaking Jews: novels, poems and books of religious teaching.
In The Spirit of Judaism she wrote about faith as something felt and lived in the heart and the home, not only kept by rule.

teach.h: THE WOMEN OF ISRAEL, ONE BY ONE.
teach.b: In The Women of Israel she went through the Bible woman by woman, Sarah, Rebekah, Miriam, Deborah, Ruth, Hannah and on, telling their stories for Jewish women readers.
Part of her point was an answer. Some writers of her day claimed that Judaism held women low. She went back to the text and said, in effect: look at these women, and how the Torah speaks of them.
A verse from the last chapter of Proverbs fits the whole project: "She openeth her mouth with wisdom; And the law of kindness is on her tongue."

She also wrote a novel, The Vale of Cedars, about Jews in Spain who had to hide their faith, the history her own family carried. And she taught: with her mother she kept a small school for boys at home.
Her health was poor, and she died young, while traveling in Germany. Her books kept being read after her.

Now look back at the week: the women who were always there, a seamstress who started a school, a rabbi in Berlin, a girl at a lectern, the debates that continue, learning that grows, and today a writer.
Each one made her own place inside the tradition, and wanted it heard.

how: Grace Aguilar's books are read today in Jewish women's history and literature courses, and her retellings of biblical women are studied as an early example of Jewish women interpreting scripture for one another.

games.q: you're Grace Aguilar. some of the English books on the Bible your Jewish neighbors read were written to persuade them to leave Judaism. what do you do?
o: write your own books, in English, from inside the tradition.
games.why: she wrote them herself, in English: The Spirit of Judaism, The Women of Israel, and more, so Jewish women could hear the Bible's women from one of their own.

practice: Recall a book, a poem, an essay or even a letter by a woman that has stayed with you, and bring back one line or one image from it as best you can. Let it sit in you for a while.
If nothing comes, that's an answer too; Grace Aguilar's books are old enough to be free to read.
